Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Breast Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Breast cancer is the disease every radiation oncology student needs to know cold: it is extremely common and, in most cases, highly curable. Before anatomy, imaging, or treatment, get three things straight: how common it is, how it's classified biologically, and what raises a person's risk.

How Common Is Breast Cancer?

1 in 8

Lifetime risk for a US woman. The most common cancer in women (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer).

#2 cause of death

The 2nd most common cause of cancer death in women, after lung cancer.

~90% screen-detected

Most cancers are found on a screening mammogram in a patient with no symptoms.

The gap between how common breast cancer is and how rarely it's fatal reflects screening (cancers are caught early) and effective multimodality treatment. The ~10% that present clinically usually come in with a painless mass. Pain, nipple discharge, nipple retraction, or an axillary node with no breast primary are less common presentations.

Classifying Breast Cancer: Hormone Receptors and HER2

Breast cancer is a family of diseases defined by two biomarkers checked on every tumor: hormone receptor (HR) status (ER/PR) and HER2 status. Together they decide which systemic therapy works and strongly shape prognosis. With the proliferation marker Ki-67, they define four molecular subtypes:

Molecular SubtypeER/PRHER2Ki-67Approx. Prevalence
Luminal APositiveNegative<14%~70%
Luminal BPositive+/−≥14%~10%
HER2-enrichedNegativeOverexpressed/amplified—~10%
Basal-likeNegativeNegative—~10%
Best prognosis
Luminal A

HR+, HER2−, low Ki-67. Slow-growing and responds to endocrine therapy.

Worst prognosis
Basal-like (mostly triple-negative)

No targets for endocrine or HER2 therapy. More common in BRCA1 carriers and younger patients.

The paradox: the most aggressive subtypes (HER2-enriched and basal-like) respond best to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

This means a high pathologic complete response (pCR) rate and a good long-term prognosis don't always go together.

Histologic Subtypes

  • Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC), now called invasive carcinoma of no special type: about 80% of invasive cancers.
  • Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC): 5–10%. Loses E-cadherin, grows in single-file lines, is often hard to see on mammogram, and is more often multicentric and bilateral. See the Anatomy section for the duct vs lobule picture.
  • Special types (tubular, mucinous/colloid, medullary, papillary, cribriform) need a >90% dominant pattern. Tubular and mucinous have an excellent prognosis; medullary is linked to BRCA1 and younger age.

Risk Factors

Most risk factors come down to longer estrogen exposure. The rest are personal or family history.

1
Estrogen Exposure

Female sex, older age, early menarche, late menopause (>55), nulliparity, first birth after 30, no breastfeeding, hormone replacement therapy.

2
Lifestyle

Postmenopausal obesity (fat makes estrogen), alcohol, high-fat diet, sedentary lifestyle.

3
Personal History

Prior breast cancer, DCIS or LCIS, atypical hyperplasia, dense breasts.

4
Radiation

Chest radiation at a young age (e.g., mantle field for Hodgkin lymphoma). Relevant to every radiation oncologist.

Hereditary Cancer Syndromes

A minority of breast cancers come from inherited mutations. These change screening, risk-reducing surgery, and sometimes radiation choices (for example, partial breast irradiation is generally avoided in known BRCA carriers).

SyndromeGene / LocusInheritanceAssociation
BRCA117q21Autosomal dominant30–50% lifetime risk; more often triple-negative
BRCA213q12Autosomal dominant50–60% lifetime risk; also male breast cancer
Li-FraumeniTP53, 17pAutosomal dominantAlso sarcoma, leukemia, brain, adrenocortical carcinoma; avoid radiation when possible (second cancers)
CowdenPTEN, 10q23Autosomal dominantHamartomas
Ataxia-telangiectasiaATM, 11q22Autosomal recessiveIncreased breast cancer risk; radiosensitivity
Peutz-JeghersSTK11Autosomal dominantIncreased breast cancer risk
Self-check: which two syndromes should make a radiation oncologist pause before treating?▾

Li-Fraumeni (TP53), because of a high risk of radiation-induced second cancers, and ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM, homozygous), because of severe radiosensitivity. In Li-Fraumeni, mastectomy is often preferred so radiation can be avoided.

Clinical Pearl

BRCA1 vs BRCA2: BRCA1 has a somewhat lower lifetime risk (30–50%) but is strongly linked to triple-negative cancer. BRCA2 has a higher lifetime risk (50–60%), behaves more like sporadic hormone-positive disease, and raises male breast cancer risk.

High-Yield Summary
  • Breast cancer subtype is defined by ER/PR and HER2 status, and subtype drives both systemic therapy and prognosis.
  • HER2-enriched and triple-negative cancers have a worse prognosis but respond best to neoadjuvant chemo.
  • Invasive lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin, grows in single-file lines, and is often multicentric and hard to see on a mammogram.
  • Most risk factors come down to more lifetime estrogen exposure, plus dense breasts, prior atypia, DCIS, or LCIS, and chest radiation at a young age.
  • BRCA1 carriers tend to get triple-negative cancers, and patients with Li-Fraumeni syndrome should avoid radiation when possible.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Breast Anatomy & Lymphatic Drainage
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
Breast radiation fields aren't drawn arbitrarily. They follow where the tumor sits in the breast and the predictable nodal basins its lymph drains to. This page has two interactive modules: the breast itself (regions, side view, and duct vs lobule) and the regional lymph nodes (axillary, supraclavicular, internal mammary, and axillary levels I–III).

The Breast: Main Regions

Describing Where a Tumor Is

  • Four quadrants: upper outer (UOQ), upper inner (UIQ), lower outer (LOQ), lower inner (LIQ), plus the central (subareolar) region.
  • Clock face: a more precise location, e.g. “2 o'clock, 3 cm from the nipple.” The clock is read as if you're facing the patient, so 2 o'clock is upper outer on the left breast but upper inner on the right.
  • Axillary tail (of Spence): breast tissue extending into the axilla, part of the UOQ.
Most common
Upper Outer Quadrant

Has the most glandular tissue, so it has the most cancers (about half).

Least common
Lower Inner Quadrant

Least tissue, fewest cancers, and, like other medial tumors, most likely to drain to the internal mammary nodes.

What Lies Under the Skin

From superficial to deep: skin → glandular tissue held up by Cooper's ligaments → retromammary fat → pectoralis major → chest wall (ribs, intercostals, serratus anterior). Two staging traps live here:

  • Skin dimpling (tumor pulling on Cooper's ligaments) is not T4. Ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or peau d'orange is T4b.
  • Invading only the pectoralis muscle is not T4a. Chest wall invasion (ribs, intercostals, serratus) is T4a.

Duct vs Lobule: IDC vs ILC

Both ductal and lobular cancers start in the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU). The names describe what the cells look like and how they grow. The key biology is E-cadherin, the protein that keeps cells stuck together.

Invasive Ductal (IDC / NST)Invasive Lobular (ILC)
Share~80%5–10%
E-cadherinPresent: cells stay in cohesive nestsLost: cells spread in single-file lines
On exam / imagingFirm, spiculated mass, often with calcificationsVague thickening; often missed on mammogram, may show only distortion
PatternUsually a single focusMore often multicentric and bilateral; MRI is helpful for extent
BiologyAny subtypeAlmost always ER+/HER2−, lower grade, less FDG-avid
MetastasesBone, lung, liver, brainAlso unusual sites: peritoneum, GI tract, ovaries, meninges
In situ versionDCIS: a true precursor, treated with surgery ± RTLCIS: mostly a risk marker, not treated with RT
Self-check: a mammogram was negative, but a palpable thickening is biopsied and shows single-file cells that are E-cadherin negative. What is it, and what imaging comes next?▾

Invasive lobular carcinoma. ILC is often hidden on mammogram and more often multicentric or bilateral, so a breast MRI is commonly used to define how much disease there is before surgery.

The Regional Lymph Nodes

The breast drains to four nodal regions. About 75% of lymph goes to the axilla, from every quadrant. Medial and central tumors can also drain to the internal mammary chain.

1
Axillary (Levels I–III)

The main basin for every quadrant. Split into three levels by the pectoralis minor.

2
Supraclavicular (SCV)

Above the clavicle. Involvement = cN3c, Stage IIIC: regional disease that is still curable, not M1.

3
Internal Mammary (IMN)

Next to the sternum in intercostal spaces 1–3. Treating them raises heart dose on the left.

4
Infraclavicular (Level III)

The top of the axilla, just below the clavicle. Involvement = cN3a.

The Axillary Levels: One Muscle Defines Them

Boundaries at a Glance

RegionWhere it isKey boundaryClinical N if involved
Level ILow axillaLateral to the lateral edge of the pec minor; lateral border = latissimus dorsicN1 (mobile) / cN2a (fixed)
Level IIMid axilla, includes Rotter's (interpectoral) nodesBehind the pec minor, around the axillary vesselscN1 / cN2a
Level IIIInfraclavicularMedial to the medial edge of the pec minor, up to the clavicle; top = coracoid / axillary vein under the claviclecN3a
SupraclavicularLow neckFrom the cricoid down to the clavicular head, between the SCM and scalenescN3c
Internal mammaryParasternalAlong the internal mammary vessels, intercostal spaces 1–3cN2b (alone) / cN3b (with axillary)
Lateral = I. Behind = II. Medial = III. The pectoralis minor is the whole answer.
Self-check: surgery removed levels I and II. Which regions are left for radiation to cover in comprehensive regional nodal irradiation?▾

Level III (infraclavicular), supraclavicular, and internal mammary nodes, plus any undissected axilla at risk. A standard axillary dissection removes levels I–II only.

Nerves in the Axilla (and What Happens If They're Injured)

Long Thoracic Nerve

Supplies the serratus anterior. Injury = winged scapula.

Thoracodorsal Nerve

Supplies the latissimus dorsi. Injury = weak arm extension and adduction.

Intercostobrachial Nerve

Sensory, often cut during ALND. Result = numb inner upper arm.

Brachial Plexus

Runs behind the SCV and level III targets. High nodal doses risk brachial plexopathy.

Why This Matters for Radiation Fields

  • Whole-breast tangents cover the breast and part of level I automatically.
  • “High tangents” raise the top edge to cover more of levels I–II. This is part of why skipping an axillary dissection worked in ACOSOG Z0011.
  • Regional nodal irradiation (RNI) adds a separate field to cover level III, supraclavicular, and usually the internal mammary nodes, plus any undissected axilla at risk.
High-Yield Summary
  • The upper outer quadrant is the most common tumor location, and medial or central tumors can also drain to the internal mammary nodes.
  • Both ductal and lobular cancers start in the terminal duct lobular unit; DCIS is a precursor that gets treated, while LCIS is mainly a risk marker.
  • The pectoralis minor defines the axillary levels: level I is lateral to it, level II is behind it, and level III is medial to it.
  • Infraclavicular nodes are N3a, internal mammary plus axillary nodes are N3b, and supraclavicular nodes are N3c, but all of these are regional and still curable.
  • Invasion of the pectoralis alone is not T4; chest wall invasion is T4a, and skin ulceration or peau d'orange is T4b.

Imaging.title: Breast Cancer Imaging
Imaging.html:
Imaging is how almost every breast cancer is found, characterized, and staged, and it's what radiation oncologists plan on. Each modality answers a different question. Learn which test answers which question, then the findings that make something suspicious.

ModalityThe question it answersWhen you'll see it
MammogramIs there something suspicious?Screening and diagnostic workup
UltrasoundIs it solid or a cyst? Are axillary nodes involved?Workup, biopsy guidance, axilla
MRIHow much disease is there, and in both breasts?High-risk screening, extent (e.g., ILC), response to neoadjuvant chemo
CT (simulation)Where exactly do we aim, and what do we avoid?Every radiation plan
PET/CTHas it spread to distant sites or hidden nodes?Stage III (and select stage IIB) disease, not early stage

Mammography and Ultrasound

Mammography

  • Screening uses two views per breast: craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO). The MLO is the only standard view that shows the axillary tail.
  • Diagnostic mammograms add spot compression (real mass vs overlapping tissue) and magnification (to characterize calcifications).
  • Three findings are suspicious: a spiculated mass, pleomorphic or linear-branching calcifications, and architectural distortion.
  • Linear/casting calcifications suggest high-grade (comedo) DCIS; fine granular calcifications suggest lower-grade DCIS.
BI-RADS: What Each Number Means
BI-RADSMeaningNext step
0IncompleteMore imaging
1 / 2Negative / benignRoutine screening
3Probably benign (≤2% cancer risk)Short-interval follow-up (6 months)
4Suspicious (4A/4B/4C)Biopsy
5Highly suggestive of cancer (≥95%)Biopsy
6Biopsy-proven cancerImaging used for extent and planning

Ultrasound

Not a routine screening test (except as a supplement in dense breasts). It's used to clarify a mammogram finding, guide biopsies, and check the axilla.

Suspicious
Malignant mass
  • Hypoechoic, irregular or spiculated
  • Taller than wide
  • Posterior shadowing, echogenic halo
Reassuring
Benign mass / cyst
  • Oval, circumscribed
  • Wider than tall
  • Posterior enhancement

Axillary nodes on ultrasound: a thickened cortex or loss of the fatty hilum is suspicious. A suspicious node gets an ultrasound-guided biopsy and a clip, so it can be found and removed later (important after neoadjuvant chemo).

Breast MRI

Contrast-enhanced MRI is the most sensitive breast test but only moderately specific (~72%), so it produces false positives. Use it for a reason:

  1. High-risk screening: BRCA carriers, >20–25% lifetime risk, prior chest radiation at a young age.
  2. Extent of disease: finds extra same-breast disease in ~15–25% and cancer in the other breast in ~5%. Especially useful for ILC and dense breasts.
  3. Response to neoadjuvant chemo, and an occult primary (axillary node with no breast finding).
  • Shape and margins matter most: spiculated (~100% PPV) and irregular (~97% PPV) masses are the strongest signs of cancer.
  • Kinetic curves: Type I (persistent rise) favors benign; Type II (plateau) and Type III (washout) are suspicious.
  • DCIS looks like non-mass enhancement in a segmental or linear pattern; a “clustered ring” is the most specific finding.
Self-check: why doesn't every newly diagnosed patient get a breast MRI?▾

Because its specificity is moderate. Routine MRI leads to extra biopsies and more mastectomies without improving survival or reducing re-excisions in average-risk patients. It's used when the answer will change management.

CT Simulation: The Radiation Oncologist's Scan

Every patient gets a planning CT in the treatment position, usually lying on a breast board with arms up. This is the scan you'll contour on. What to look for:

  • Lumpectomy cavity (seroma) and surgical clips: define the tumor bed for a boost or partial breast treatment.
  • Heart and LAD (left-sided cancers): major cardiac events rise about 7% per Gy of mean heart dose (Darby). Deep inspiration breath hold (DIBH) moves the heart away from the chest wall.
  • Ipsilateral lung: the slice of lung inside the tangents drives pneumonitis risk.
  • Nodal regions (level III, SCV, IMN) when regional nodal RT is planned. Including the IMN makes it harder to spare the heart and lung.
For a left-sided breast, the first question on the sim CT is: how close is the heart, and can breath hold help?

PET/CT and Systemic Staging

  • Not for early-stage disease. In stage I–II without symptoms, systemic imaging finds more false positives than metastases.
  • Use it for stage III (and consider it for select stage IIB, e.g. T3N0 or T2N1), alongside or instead of CT chest/abdomen/pelvis plus bone scan.
  • PET is good at finding hidden IMN, infraclavicular, and SCV nodes and bone metastases. Any of these can change the stage and the radiation fields.
  • Weak spot: lobular and low-grade cancers are often only faintly FDG-avid.
Self-check: PET/CT for a cT2N1 patient shows an FDG-avid supraclavicular node that is biopsy-positive. What's the new stage, and is the goal still cure?▾

cN3c, Stage IIIC. Yes, the goal is still cure: SCV nodes are regional, not distant. Treatment becomes neoadjuvant chemo, surgery, and comprehensive nodal RT including the supraclavicular fossa, with a boost to the involved node.

Special Situations

DCIS
Calcifications underestimate it

DCIS shows up as calcifications alone in 50–75% of cases. The true extent is usually larger than the calcifications, which is why DCIS needs wider margins (≥2 mm).

Inflammatory (T4d)
Skin, not a mass

Diffuse skin thickening and trabecular coarsening, often with no discrete mass. MRI best shows extent. It's a clinical diagnosis (erythema/edema of ≥1/3 of the breast, rapid onset) confirmed with a skin biopsy.

High-Yield Summary
  • The mammogram finds the cancer: a spiculated mass, pleomorphic or linear calcifications, or architectural distortion is suspicious, and BI-RADS 4 or 5 means biopsy.
  • Dense breast tissue hides cancer on a mammogram, which is why younger women with a palpable lump get an ultrasound first.
  • MRI is the most sensitive test and is used for high-risk screening, extent of disease (especially lobular cancer), and response to neoadjuvant chemo.
  • On the planning CT, find the lumpectomy cavity and clips, and for left-sided cancers check how close the heart is and whether breath hold will help.
  • PET/CT is used for stage III disease, not for early-stage breast cancer.

Workup & Staging.title: Breast Cancer Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
The breast workup goes in a set order: confirm the diagnosis with the right biopsy, characterize the biology, then decide how much staging imaging is really needed. Breast staging is unusual because it mixes anatomy (TNM) with biology (grade, ER, PR, HER2). The full AJCC tables are in a clickable set at the bottom of the page.

The Core Workup

  1. History and physical. Breast exam (size, skin changes, fixation) and the axilla, supraclavicular, and infraclavicular nodes. Ask about family history and menopausal status.
  2. Diagnostic imaging. Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound of the breast and axilla; MRI for select patients.
  3. Core needle biopsy of the breast lesion (and any suspicious node), with a clip placed. Core biopsy, not FNA, because FNA can't tell DCIS from invasive cancer.
  4. Pathology: histology, grade, ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67.
  5. Genetic counseling/testing when indicated (e.g., young age, triple-negative, strong family history, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, male breast cancer).
  6. Systemic staging only when needed (see below). Add fertility counseling for premenopausal patients who may get chemo.

Biopsy Technique

LesionBiopsy
Seen on ultrasound (most masses)Ultrasound-guided core
Calcifications onlyStereotactic (mammogram-guided) core
Seen only on MRIMRI-guided core
Skin changes / suspected inflammatory or PagetPunch biopsy of the skin

Reading the Pathology Report

ItemWhat counts
ER / PR<1% = negative; 1–10% = “low positive”
HER2 (IHC)0 or 1+ = negative; 2+ = equivocal → FISH; 3+ = positive
Ki-67Proliferation index; low (<14%) fits Luminal A
Nottingham gradeTubules + nuclear pleomorphism + mitoses, each 1–3. Sum 3–5 = G1, 6–7 = G2, 8–9 = G3
LVSI / EICLymphovascular invasion; extensive intraductal component (>25% DCIS)
MarginsInvasive: no tumor on ink. DCIS: ≥2 mm

Who Needs Systemic Staging Imaging?

Stage I–II, no symptoms
No routine body imaging

Labs and imaging only if symptoms or abnormal labs point to metastasis. Scans find more false positives than cancers here.

Stage III (T3N1, T4, N2–3)
Full staging

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + bone scan, or PET/CT. Brain MRI if symptoms. Echocardiogram before anthracyclines or trastuzumab.

The Staging Framework: T, N, and M

Same scaffold as other sites, with a few breast-specific twists. Learn these high-yield points and look up the rest in the tables.

T-Stage: Size, Then Skin and Chest Wall

  • Tis — DCIS (or Paget disease without an underlying tumor). LCIS is no longer staged as Tis.
  • T1 — ≤2 cm (T1mi ≤1 mm, T1a >1–5 mm, T1b >5–10 mm, T1c >10–20 mm)
  • T2 — >2 to 5 cm
  • T3 — >5 cm
  • T4 — any size with:
    • T4a — chest wall invasion (not pectoralis muscle alone)
    • T4b — skin: ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or peau d'orange edema
    • T4c — both T4a and T4b
    • T4d — inflammatory carcinoma
Breast T-stage breakpoints are 2 cm and 5 cm. Skin or chest wall = T4, whatever the size.

Clinical N-Stage: Which Nodes, and Are They Fixed?

Breast N-stage depends on which basin is involved, as much as how many nodes:

  • cN0 — no regional nodes
  • cN1 — movable ipsilateral level I/II axillary nodes
  • cN2:
    • cN2a — level I/II axillary nodes fixed or matted
    • cN2b — internal mammary nodes without axillary nodes
  • cN3:
    • cN3a — infraclavicular (level III) nodes
    • cN3b — internal mammary plus axillary nodes
    • cN3c — supraclavicular nodes

Pathologic N-Stage: Count the Nodes

  • pN0(i+) — isolated tumor cells, ≤0.2 mm (still counts as N0)
  • pN1mi — micrometastasis, >0.2 to 2 mm
  • pN1a — 1–3 axillary nodes (at least one >2 mm)
  • pN2a — 4–9 axillary nodes
  • pN3a — ≥10 axillary nodes, or any infraclavicular (level III) node
The pathologic node counts that drive radiation decisions: 1–3 (pN1), 4–9 (pN2), 10+ (pN3).

M-Stage

M0 or M1. Bone is the most common distant site. Remember: supraclavicular nodes are N3c, not M1. A contralateral axillary or SCV node, however, counts as M1.

Stage Groups (Anatomic)

StageT / N / M
0Tis N0
IAT1 N0
IBT0–1 N1mi
IIAT0–1 N1, or T2 N0
IIBT2 N1, or T3 N0
IIIAT0–2 N2, or T3 N1–2
IIIBT4 N0–2
IIICAny T, N3
IVM1
Stage it: 3.2 cm tumor, two movable level I axillary nodes on exam, no metastases.▾

cT2 cN1 M0 = Stage IIB. 3.2 cm is T2 (2–5 cm); movable level I/II nodes are cN1.

Stage it: 1.5 cm tumor with a biopsy-proven supraclavicular node.▾

cT1c cN3c M0 = Stage IIIC. Any N3 is IIIC regardless of how small the primary is, and it is still curable.

Stage it: 6 cm tumor with peau d'orange over a third of the breast, rapid onset, and diffuse redness.▾

T4d (inflammatory breast cancer), at least Stage IIIB. Diffuse erythema and edema of ≥1/3 of the breast with rapid onset make it inflammatory, not just T4b skin involvement.

Prognostic Stage: Where Biology Comes In

AJCC 8 has a second, prognostic stage that adjusts the anatomic stage using grade, ER, PR, HER2, and sometimes the Oncotype DX score. It's the stage used in the US for patients who get standard treatment.

  • Favorable biology (ER+, PR+, HER2+ or low grade) can lower the stage.
  • Triple-negative disease often raises the stage.
  • A T1–2 N0, ER+/HER2− tumor with an Oncotype score <11 is staged IA regardless of size.

You don't need to memorize the prognostic table. Know that it exists and which direction biology pushes the stage.

Stage Prefixes You'll See

c

Clinical: exam and imaging before treatment.

p

Pathologic: after upfront surgery.

yp

After neoadjuvant therapy. ypT0 ypN0 = pathologic complete response (pCR).

Clinical Pearl

After neoadjuvant chemo, radiation decisions use both the clinical stage before chemo and the yp stage after surgery. Always write down the pre-chemo cT and cN, because they're lost once the tumor shrinks.

Staging Tables

These are the AJCC 8th edition breast definitions, the ones reproduced in the NCCN Breast Cancer Guidelines. Click a tab or use the arrows. Stage the patient here, then find the matching treatment table at the bottom of Treatment Paradigms.

The AJCC 8 prognostic stage starts from the anatomic stage and adjusts it using grade, ER, PR, and HER2. The full table has dozens of rows; these are the patterns to recognize.

Biology lowers the stageER+ / PR+ / HER2+ tumors, and low-grade ER+ tumors, are often downstaged (e.g., some anatomic IIIA become IB–IIA)
Biology raises the stageTriple-negative and high-grade tumors are often upstaged (e.g., T1N0 grade 3 triple-negative becomes IB)
Genomic overrideT1–2 N0, ER+/HER2− with Oncotype DX recurrence score <11 = Stage IA
When it appliesPathologic prognostic stage is for patients who had surgery first; clinical prognostic stage for everyone else
High-Yield Summary
  • Workup is a diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound, a core biopsy with a clip, ER/PR/HER2 and grade, and an exam of the axilla and supraclavicular nodes.
  • Body imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and bone scan, or PET/CT) is only for stage III disease or symptoms.
  • T stage breaks at 2 cm and 5 cm, with T4a for chest wall invasion, T4b for skin involvement, and T4d for inflammatory cancer.
  • Clinical N1 is movable axillary nodes, N2 is fixed axillary nodes or internal mammary nodes alone, and N3 is infraclavicular, internal mammary plus axillary, or supraclavicular nodes.
  • Any N3 disease is stage IIIC and still treated for cure, while contralateral axillary nodes are metastatic (M1).

Treatment Paradigms.title: Breast Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
Breast cancer treatment is built from three pillars: surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy. Almost every radiation decision comes down to three questions:

1
What surgery?

After lumpectomy, the breast almost always gets RT. After mastectomy, RT is only for high-risk disease.

2
What are the nodes?

N0: treat the breast. N+: add the regional nodes. SCV or N3: treat everything and boost the node.

3
What's the biology?

Subtype picks the drugs (endocrine, anti-HER2, chemo ± immunotherapy) and whether chemo comes before or after surgery.

The Framework: Who Gets What Radiation

The breast radiation framework

Each step adds to the one above it. Find the first step that fits your patient.

0
DCIS after lumpectomy
Whole-breast RT; can be omitted for low-risk DCIS.
1
Invasive, node-negative, after lumpectomy
Whole-breast RT ± boost. Partial breast RT or omission for select low-risk patients.
2
Node-positive
Breast + regional nodal irradiation (RNI).
3
Locally advanced: T4, inflammatory, N3 (SCV)
Neoadjuvant chemo, surgery, then comprehensive nodal RT with a boost to gross nodes.
4
After mastectomy
PMRT to the chest wall + nodes only for high-risk features (T3–4, ≥4 nodes, positive margin).

The Role of Surgery

Breast-conserving
Lumpectomy + RT

Same survival as mastectomy. Preferred for most early-stage patients, and radiation is part of the package.

Removes the breast
Mastectomy

For patients who can't have (or don't want) a lumpectomy. RT depends on risk (Paradigm 4).

NSABP B-06 / Milan

Lumpectomy + RT gave the same survival as mastectomy.

EBCTCG meta-analysis

RT after lumpectomy halved recurrence and prevented about 1 breast cancer death for every 4 recurrences prevented.

Lumpectomy isn't a good option for inflammatory cancer, diffuse suspicious calcifications, persistently positive margins, or patients who can't get RT (prior chest RT, pregnancy, active scleroderma/lupus, Li-Fraumeni).

The Axilla: Sentinel Node vs Dissection

Clinically node-negative
→
Sentinel node biopsy
→
1–2 positive: usually no dissection

Sentinel node biopsy (SLNB) is standard for a clinically negative axilla. A full axillary dissection (ALND) is now kept for bulky or matted nodes, inflammatory cancer, and nodes that stay positive after neoadjuvant chemo, because it causes lymphedema in about 20–25% of patients.

ACOSOG Z0011

cT1–2 cN0 with 1–2 positive sentinel nodes, treated with lumpectomy + whole-breast RT: skipping ALND did not change survival.

AMAROS

For a positive sentinel node, axillary RT instead of ALND gave the same axillary control with about half the lymphedema.

Neoadjuvant (before surgery)
  • HER2+ or triple-negative, ≥cT2 or cN+
  • Locally advanced: T4, N2–3, inflammatory
  • To shrink a tumor enough for lumpectomy
Adjuvant (after surgery)
  • Most HR+/HER2− early-stage cancers
  • Chemo decided by final pathology and a genomic score (Oncotype DX)

Chemo is never given at the same time as RT. Anti-HER2 drugs and endocrine therapy can run during RT.

DCIS (Stage 0)

  • Lumpectomy + whole-breast RT is standard. RT halves in-breast recurrence (about half of recurrences are invasive) but does not change survival.
  • RT can be omitted for low-risk DCIS: small, low or intermediate grade, widely clear margins.
  • Mastectomy for DCIS needs no RT.
NSABP B-17 / EORTC 10853

Adding RT after lumpectomy for DCIS cut in-breast recurrence in half, with no survival difference.

RTOG 9804

Even in low-risk DCIS, RT lowered recurrence, but the absolute benefit was small, so omission is reasonable.

Paradigm 1: Node-Negative After Lumpectomy

  1. Whole-breast RT, hypofractionated: 40 Gy / 15 fx (3 weeks) or 26 Gy / 5 fx (1 week).
  2. Add a boost to the tumor bed for age ≤50, high grade, or a positive margin.
  3. Partial breast RT for low-risk patients: older, ≤2 cm, N0, ER+, negative margins.
  4. Omit RT for age ≥65–70, T1N0, ER+, negative margins, taking endocrine therapy.
START B / FAST-Forward

40 Gy / 15 fx, and then 26 Gy / 5 fx, matched longer courses for control and side effects. Hypofractionation is now standard.

CALGB 9343 / PRIME II

Older patients with small ER+ N0 tumors on endocrine therapy: skipping RT raised local recurrence slightly but did not change survival.

Try it: 45-year-old, 1.4 cm ER+ grade 2 IDC, lumpectomy with negative margins, 0/2 sentinel nodes. What radiation?▾

Whole-breast RT plus a tumor bed boost. She's node-negative, so no nodal fields, but age ≤50 is a boost indication and she's too young for omission.

Paradigm 2: Node-Positive

Once nodes are involved, the regional nodes (level III, supraclavicular, internal mammary) join the target. The exception is Z0011-type patients (1–2 positive sentinel nodes, lumpectomy): whole-breast RT alone, often with high tangents.

MA.20 / EORTC 22922

Adding regional nodal RT for node-positive (and high-risk N0) patients improved disease-free survival and reduced distant metastases.

A dissected axilla (levels I–II) usually isn't retreated, because RT on top of ALND sharply raises lymphedema.

Paradigm 3: Locally Advanced (T4, Inflammatory, SCV Nodes)

Supraclavicular (cN3c) or infraclavicular (cN3a) nodes, T4 tumors, and inflammatory cancer are Stage III, not metastatic. The goal is cure with all three pillars:

  • RT is based on the pre-chemo stage, so it is given even after a complete response.
  • Inflammatory (T4d) always gets a modified radical mastectomy (no lumpectomy, no SLNB) and PMRT with bolus.
Try it: cT2 cN3c triple-negative cancer has a complete response to chemo (ypT0 ypN0) and a lumpectomy. Can radiation be skipped?▾

No. RT follows the worst stage. She gets whole-breast RT plus comprehensive nodal RT including the supraclavicular fossa.

Paradigm 4: After Mastectomy (PMRT)

After mastectomy the question flips to “is the risk high enough to need RT?”

PMRT indicated
  • T3–T4
  • ≥4 positive nodes
  • Positive margin
  • Stage III before chemo, or ypN+ after
Strongly consider
  • 1–3 positive nodes
  • T3N0: individualize

PMRT treats the chest wall + regional nodes, with bolus when the skin is at risk. Radiation raises implant complications, so reconstruction is planned with the RT team.

High-Yield Summary
  • Lumpectomy plus radiation gives the same survival as mastectomy, so the breast almost always gets RT after a lumpectomy.
  • Node-negative patients get whole-breast RT (40 Gy in 15 fractions or 26 Gy in 5), with a boost for young age, high grade, or a positive margin.
  • Node-positive patients get the regional nodes added, but 1 to 2 positive sentinel nodes after lumpectomy do not need an axillary dissection (Z0011).
  • Locally advanced disease gets neoadjuvant chemo, surgery, and comprehensive nodal RT, even after a complete response.
  • After mastectomy, RT is given for T3 to T4 tumors, 4 or more positive nodes, or a positive margin, and is strongly considered for 1 to 3 nodes.
